beginner.headline: Driver Wants Lower Tax on Fuel
beginner.brief: The BBC asked people how the government's new money plans affect their lives. Dave Herbert works as a driver. He spends about £350 a month on petrol for work and his own trips. Dave wanted a lower tax on fuel, but the government did not lower it. He feels angry about this. A 19-year-old woman is looking for work. She wants businesses to get more money so they can give jobs to more young people. Robert Portlock lives with his parents and wants to move out. He says rent for a small flat would take most of his monthly pay. Chloe lives with her son and pays about £200 a month for gas and electricity. She tries to spend no more than £40 a week on food. She thinks the government's £100 energy payment will help her.

intermediate.headline: Households React Differently to the Budget
intermediate.brief: People with different incomes told the BBC how the government's Budget, its plan for taxes and spending, could affect their finances. Dave Herbert, a professional driver, says fuel prices have been extremely high this year. He says his monthly petrol costs are around £350, between 40% and 50% higher than at the start of the year. Dave was disappointed because the Budget did not include the cut in fuel duty, a tax on fuel, that he wanted. Emily Nelson has been unable to find a job since leaving college last year. She wants more funding for businesses so they can employ more young people, as well as more money for training. Robert Portlock wants to leave his parents' home, but he does not think he can afford to live independently. He says a small flat in his area would cost about two-thirds of his monthly wage in rent. Chloe has cut back on luxuries, including cinema visits, and tries to keep her weekly food shopping within £40. However, Chloe feels hopeful about the Budget because she believes small changes can help her. She says cuts to standing charges, the fixed costs on gas bills, and a £100 energy payment will help her. A higher earner wanted higher taxes for people with large incomes like his own, but says the Budget offered nothing on this. He argues that better roads, hospitals and schools require more tax income.

advanced.headline: Budget Divides Households Over Relief, Opportunity and Fairness
advanced.brief: BBC News asked people with annual incomes ranging from £4,062 to £150,000 to assess this year's Budget. Dave says he now pays around £350 a month for fuel for work and personal use, between 40% and 50% more than at the start of the year. With an already strained household budget, Dave says higher fuel costs leave him little financial headroom. The main rate of fuel duty, a tax on fuel, remains frozen at 57.95p per litre, but Dave disputes the suggestion that maintaining the rate amounts to giving motorists something. He wanted a reduction in fuel duty and was disappointed that the Budget offered none. Emily is frustrated that the government will await the outcome of a review of youth unemployment before legislating next year. For the employment scheme, she favours reducing the eligibility threshold for time spent seeking work from 18 months to a year. For Robert, renting a small flat would be his biggest concern, since it would absorb about two-thirds of his monthly wage. His car costs £750 a month in finance, insurance, fuel and tax, yet he says he needs it for his commute to Newcastle Airport. Chloe values paying a below-market rate for housing association accommodation, although she says sharing bills previously made life easier. She welcomes the Budget, saying that even small changes give her hope. Another interviewee wants higher earners such as himself to pay more tax in the interests of redistribution. He says each of his daughters will begin working life with £45,000 to £60,000 in debt, with interest compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 a year. While he accepts paying for university degrees, he argues that interest should be waived or capped below 1%. Christine says she finds it difficult to balance the books and increasingly draws on savings to support herself. She is unsure whether removing fixed charges from gas bills will benefit her, because transferring those costs to the unit rate, the price charged for each unit of gas consumed, could offset the saving. She nevertheless expects the £100 household energy allowance to help over the winter. Her overall assessment is that she may end up financially unchanged, rather than better off.
